one_liner: One CI run of the Alya suite: Bun 1.4.2 finishes depth-14 binary trees in 98.3 ms, against 126.3 ms for gcc -O2 C using malloc and free per node.
what_it_does: This is not a library but one row of the Alya language's cross-language suite, where the same binary-trees program is written in C, JavaScript, Python and Alya. The JS version (cross_lang/collections/binary_trees.js) builds about 6.35 million three-field TreeNode objects through a constructor function and leaves them to the garbage collector. The C version mallocs a 24-byte node for each one and frees every tree with a recursive free_tree. The runner (cross_lang/runner.ts, which itself runs under Bun) compiles the C with gcc -O2, spawns each program as a separate process 11 times, and reports the median wall-clock time of the last 10.
how_it_is_fast: The suite names no mechanism. The gap comes from memory management, not code generation: C makes one malloc and one free call per node, plus a second recursive walk to free each tree, about 6.35 million of each (20 ns per node at 126.3 ms, process start included; derived from page data). JavaScriptCore allocates from a segregated-storage heap. Its non-moving Riptide collector is generational through sticky mark bits, so an eden collection visits only new objects and remembered-set entries, and dead short-lived trees are reclaimed by sweeping with no per-object free call. Allocation-bound tree code with the same shape also lets the GC'd runtimes beat malloc/free C in the benchLANG and LangArena sibling entries.
when_to_use: As one small data point that a JIT plus a generational GC can beat naive per-node malloc/free in C on allocation-bound code with tiny, short-lived nodes (24-byte structs, roughly 6.35 million allocations).
As a prompt to check the allocator in your own C or C++ tree code: the C program here mallocs and frees one node at a time, at -O2 without -march or LTO.
As a small MIT-licensed, four-language test kit: each program prints one integer that the runner checks against a fixed expected value (-43682 for binary trees).
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Bun beats C in general: C wins the other 13 rows of the same table, by 2.5x (linked list, 3.0 vs 7.4 ms) up to 9.2x (matrix multiply, 1.3 vs 12.0 ms) (derived from page data).
As a stable number: in earlier snapshots of the same CI job, C beats Bun on binary trees in 4 of 14 runs (see gotchas).
Against a C program that uses an arena or pool allocator, frees nothing before exit, or builds with -O3 -march=native: none of these was measured here.

When memory or footprint matters: the README's Bun figures (about 92 MB runtime, about 24 ms cold start, about 36.5 MB RSS) are hard-coded strings in runner.ts, not measurements, and Bun's RSS is never recorded for this workload.
As a sub-100 ms latency figure: these are whole-process times on a shared, noisy VM whose CPU model is not recorded.

integration.form: benchmark script (single-file JavaScript, run with 'bun run binary_trees.js')
integration.dependencies: Bun runtime (1.4.2 as measured); the full runner also needs gcc, Python 3.12, Rust and the Alya compiler (alya-lang/alya, built from the develop branch in CI)
integration.min_toolchain: Bun 1.4.2 as measured (CI installs whatever oven-sh/setup-bun@v2 resolves to); C baseline gcc 13.3.0 at -O2
integration.platforms: Published numbers are from GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest x64 (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS) only; the workflow can also target ARM64 Linux, Windows and macOS runners, but those results are not in the README

gotchas: Harness flaw, the result flips between CI runs. I read 14 README snapshots written by the same workflow (2026-09-18 to 2026-10-08; all Bun 1.4.2, gcc 13.3.0 -O2, Ubuntu 24.04.5 x64, one warm-up plus 10 runs). The C/Bun time ratio ranges from 0.84 to 1.31, and C wins in 4 of them: 5ff783f (C 60.0 vs Bun 64.6 ms), 37e3b6c (70.2 vs 83.3), 3ee8a72 (70.5 vs 82.4) and e382f6c (106.0 vs 113.4). In the fast snapshots every row speeds up (fib C 1.4 to 1.6 ms vs 2.3), C's binary-trees time drops about 1.8x (126 to 70 ms) and Bun's only about 1.17x (97 to 83 ms). Which machine the shared runner draws decides the winner, and the runner never records the CPU model.

Unequal work: inside the timed process, C calls free on every node through a recursive free_tree (about 6.35 million free calls plus an extra full traversal of each tree). The JS version frees nothing and leaves dead trees to the GC and to process exit. Only the build and check passes are the same algorithm.

Whole-process wall clock: spawnSync timing of programs that run about 100 ms. Bun's start-up, parsing and JIT tiering fall inside its 98.3 ms, and C's process start falls inside its 126.3 ms. Each language's 10 runs are taken back to back, not interleaved.

Output check: a substring match on -43682 that only warns, although the runner then exits 1 and the CI commit step does not run, so committed numbers did pass the check. The verifier's '1.9x to 9x' range for the other 13 C wins is really 2.5x to 9.2x on the 2026-10-08 table.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Cite the benchLANG Bun row (0.816 s vs C 1.010 s built at -O3 -march=native -flto) or LangArena Binarytrees::Obj (Bun 0.973 s vs the best C/C++ build at 2.098 s) instead. They show the same Bun-beats-malloc effect against stronger C builds in second-long runs; this row is only a 100 ms CI data point whose winner changes with the runner.
verified_claims_summary: On a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest x64 runner (Ubuntu 24.04.5, CPU not recorded, run of 2026-10-08), the median of 10 whole-process runs after one warm-up was 98.3 ms for 'bun run binary_trees.js' (Bun 1.4.2). The same depth-14 binary-trees program in C, built with gcc 13.3.0 -O2 with malloc and free per node, took 126.3 ms: about 1.28x (derived from page data). Earlier snapshots of the same job range from Bun 1.31x faster to C 1.19x faster.
status_note: Active: CI-generated README commits continue to 2026-10-08 (51 commits, 0 stars, MIT). The suite exists to promote the Alya language, so treat it as a reference data point, not something to adopt; the C and JS sources have not changed since the initial commit on 2026-09-11.
